claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle failure.
Dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The local stress concentrations associated with dislocation pile-ups promote microcracking and catastrophic failure during straining.
High-pressure and high-temperature treatment in a hexahedron-anvil apparatus will refine the alloy's dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Rapid quenching after the high-pressure and high-temperature treatment will preserve the refined microstructure.
The treatment will modify internal boundaries so that they discourage dislocation pile-ups.
The combination of high pressure and elevated temperature activates dynamic recovery in the alloy.
The combination of high pressure and elevated temperature activates dynamic recrystallization in the alloy.
Dynamic recovery and recrystallization transform the dual-phase lamellar colonies into a more homogeneous structure.
The more homogeneous refined structure reduces dislocation pile-ups and associated stress-concentration regions.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups and stress concentrations delays microcrack initiation and catastrophic failure.
The treatment will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will retain or increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
More uniformly distributed dislocations and reduced stress concentrations are responsible for the predicted combination of greater ductility and retained or increased strength.
Insufficient pressure may prevent the desired microstructural refinement and mechanical-property improvement.
Excessively slow quenching may cause grain coarsening and may leave mechanical properties unchanged or worsen them.
Dynamic recrystallization under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions is a well-established mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits strength merely to remain comparable to the untreated state, whereas the falsification rule can be read as requiring a statistically significant strength improvement. Under that reading, unchanged strength would both satisfy the prediction and falsify the hypothesis.
